To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

unsupervised learning can be used as an effective pre-training strategy to improve the generalization of a deep network on a target task, and that the pre-training can be done in a domain-independent manner, i.e. without access to any labeled data from the target distribution.

(a) unsupervised pre-trained representations are useful for transfer learning, because they allow the learning algorithm to make more informed use of the available labeled examples, by exploiting the information that has been captured by the representations, and (b) unsupervised representation learning is a powerful tool for disentangling the unknown factors of the training distribution, and hence for improving transfer learning performance.

1) unsupervised pretraining is a useful tool for transfer learning; 2) it is important to pretrain on a task that is structurally related, rather than just correlated, to the task of interest; and 3) the pretraining task can be as simple as predicting the next word in a sequence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: How to learn useful representations from unlabeled data, and exploit these representations for improved learning in the transfer learning setting?
the following questions: (1) What are good representations for unsupervised and transfer learning?
the following three questions: • What is the role of unsupervised learning in deep learning algorithms?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the main advantage of unsupervised pre-trained representations is that they allow us to transfer the knowledge learned about one task to another task, when we do not have access to the training distribution of the task that we are interested in.

the use of pre-trained representations can improve performance, especially in transfer learning scenarios, but the extent to which this is true depends on the details of the problem, the architecture, and the training procedure.

unsupervised learning is not a panacea but a very useful tool for improving generalization in the transfer learning setup, and that it is particularly useful when the task of interest is related to a distribution that is very different from the training distribution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
unsupervised pretraining of deep neural networks (DNNs) can help to learn better models for a wide range of tasks.
unsupervised pretraining of deep neural networks can be a powerful tool for transfer learning, but it is also important to understand when it works and when it does not.

we have proposed a framework for unsupervised and semi-supervised learning of representation that is based on the idea of learning an energy function, which can be viewed as an implicit model of the data distribution, and which can be used to define a generative model for data.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, when the input distribution is structured in a way that can be captured by a deep generative model, then unsupervised pretraining can lead to representations with better transferability properties, compared to random initialization of the parameters of the deep network.
, in order to exploit unsupervised pretraining in transfer learning, we need to ensure that the representations learned are disentangled.

unsupervised pre-trained representations can be very helpful for transfer learning, even when they are learned from a distribution P (x), which is structurally unrelated to the target task P (y|x), as long as the two distributions share some unknown factors of variation.
